newsitem.title: PERU: Peru siege site a sad shell of former grandeur.
newsitem.headline: Peru siege site a sad shell of former grandeur.

text.p: The Japanese ambassador's residence used to be the grandest building on the block. Not any more.

Built as a mockup of the antebellum home in "Gone with the Wind", the collonaded mansion in a quiet street of the upscale San Isidro district is now a burnt-out shell, littered with the debris of battle and painful memories.
Public opinion is sharply divided on what to do with the residence now the 126-day hostage drama is over.
While many feel it is a macabre wreck that should be razed to the ground, others said that despite a tragic recent past, it can still be restored to former glory.
"It's very beautiful and it's worth it to show we're not afraid," said Elizabeth Mercado who lives opposite the two- storey building.

But there is a growing feeling that the crumbling structure, where 14 rebels, two army officers and one local judge lost their lives on Tuesday, should stand as a monument to Latin America's longest hostage standoff.
"They should leave it as it is ... and keep it as a symbol of peace, a symbol of Peru's fight against terrorism," said Antonio Bazo, another neighbour.
Japanese officials were typically understated about the building's future.

"We may have to abandon the official residence and look for another one somewhere else," a Japanese Foreign Ministry official told Reuters. "It was so badly damaged from the floor to the walls and ceilings. There are even tunnels right beneath the floor. That's very bad."
It was the spectacular assault to end the standoff that gave the diplomat's home its final coup de grace.

Television images of a triumphant President Alberto Fujimori inspecting the scene of his most spectacular victory, showed a massive crater in the downstairs reception room from which troops emerged to surprise rebel leader Nestor Cerpa and seven comrades playing soccer with a ball improvised from socks wrapped by tape.

Charred furniture, shattered glass, doors and hand grenades were strewn all around and the walls potted with bullet marks. Climbing up the blood-stained staircase, which led to the ambassador's once-private chambers, Fujimori paused as he at last came face-to-face with his mortal enemy, Cerpa, lying face up, a bullet hole in his head and a gash in his neck.
Fujimori later revealed the key to the attack had been a warren of tunnels, excavated over several weeks under cover of military marching tunes, which criss-crossed the whole property.
It was all so different on Dec. 17.

Ambassador Morihisa Aoki's home was at its resplendent best. Bow-tied waiters attended to Peru's rich and powerful as the Japanese embassy threw its annual bash to commemorate the 68th birthday of Emperor Akihito.
Patio doors opened onto the rear garden where a huge tent housed a banquet of fine food and drink. A 30-foot (10-meter) fir tree nearby was decked with Christmas decorations.
But with a loud blast, 14 Marxist rebels burst into the party through a hole in an outer wall and changed the building forever.
For 18 weeks the Tupac Amaru Revolutionary Movement (MRTA) gunmen held out inside the building with their prized human booty.
Fearful of a counter attack, the rebels mined and booby- trapped the whole property, turning it into what Fujimori described as a "bunker".
Even before Tuesday's explosive raid by crack Peruvian troops who secured the release of all but one of the 72 hostages, Aoki's home was showing signs of wear.
Its parched dry gardens stood in sharp contrast with the plush lawns of neighbouring properties and the lavish banquet had been scavenged away by birds and cats.
A Reuters photographer who entered the residence for an impromptu news conference with Cerpa on Dec. 31, described a home turned upside down.

Furniture had been piled up against the walls and doors, field toilets had been brought in to relieve pressure on the overtaxed bathrooms, revolutionary slogans were daubed on the walls and discarded food and litter were strewn over the floor.
Freed Jesuit Priest Juan Julio Wicht recounted that the rubbish attracted mice that crawled over the hostages as they tried to sleep.
"The mice were all over us. It was so nauseous and disgusting that the number of rodents didn't let us sleep."
